Ben had started going out alone, obsessed with finding the rarest fungi, ignoring the field guide's warnings. The doctors are still pumping his stomach. I pace the length of the linoleum floor, my fingernails digging half-moons into my palms. Every time the double doors swing open, my heart stutters, and my breath catches in a tight, painful knot. I close my eyes and see the deadly white caps of the destroying angel mushrooms scattered on his desk. I fall into a plastic chair, burying my face in my hands, unable to breathe.

Sarah stood in the doorway of the basement gym, her arms crossed tightly over her stomach as if holding herself together. The rhythmic, punishing clang of heavy iron plates echoed off the concrete walls. Her son, barely sixteen, grunted under a barbell bending from the absurd weight. Sarah winced with every rep, her jaw clamped shut so tightly her teeth ached. She had bought him his first set of dumbbells to help his posture. Now, his veins bulged unnaturally against skin marred by stretch marks, his locker stuffed with unlabelled vials. She watched him rack the weight, his nose bleeding slightly from the exertion. Sarah backed away into the hallway shadow, sliding down the wall until she hit the floor. She bit down hard on the sleeve of her sweater, stifling a ragged sob as the metal clanged violently again.

The neoprene wetsuit hanging in the garage feels like a ghost. I spent twenty years exploring wrecks, bringing up rusted coins to show little Clara. I made the ocean magic for her. Now, I track her boat on my laptop, my stomach churning with a sour, burning acid. She is diving the Mariana Trench edge today, pushing past recreational limits, chasing deeper, darker abysses. I haven't slept more than two hours a night since she bought the rebreather gear. I sit at the kitchen island, rhythmically tapping my pen until it snaps in half, ink staining my fingers. I dial her satellite phone again. No answer. A cold sweat breaks out across the back of my neck. I walk to the bathroom, staring at my pale, drawn face in the mirror, wondering which dive will be the one where she simply never surfaces.

The rusted detector hummed its familiar, irritating pitch from the trench in the backyard. Elias watched from the kitchen window, his fingernails digging deeply into the wooden sill. He had bought it at a garage sale, thinking it would get ten-year-old Noah out of the house. Now, the lawn was a battlefield of craters. Noah dug furiously in the freezing rain, covered in mud, ignoring his mother’s calls for dinner. Elias felt a tight band constrict across his chest. He saw the blistered, raw skin on Noah’s small hands gripping the trowel. Elias turned away from the window, pressing his back against the wall, sliding down until his knees hit his chest. He squeezed his eyes shut, but the relentless, high-pitched beep of the metal detector penetrated the walls, drilling directly into his brain. He gripped his hair, pulling hard.

Elias stared at the glowing screen until the white background burned into his retinas. "We do not see a place for this on our list," the email read. He dragged his fingernails down his scalp, feeling the harsh scrape against his skin. For the fourth night in a row, sleep felt like an impossible myth. Every time he closed his eyes, the words rearranged themselves into jagged little teeth, gnawing at the back of his mind. He paced the narrow hallway, his bare feet slapping the hardwood, his breathing ragged and uneven. A stack of his printed pages sat on the desk. He wanted to set it on fire. A dull ache throbbed behind his temples, relentless and rhythmic. He pressed the heels of his hands hard against his eye sockets until colors burst in the darkness, wishing the pressure could crush the memory of that polite, ruinous paragraph.

I grip the ceramic mug so tightly my knuckles ache, but I can't feel the heat. Through the café window, people laugh and hurry through the rain, living lives that aren't currently collapsing. My phone screen is still open to the email from HarperCollins. Every sentence of their polite decline echoes in my skull, a looping track I can’t mute. My stomach twists into tight, suffocating knots, acid rising in my throat. I want to scream, to shatter the mug against the brick wall, to tear my skin right off. Instead, I just sit here, perfectly still, while an invisible vice tightens around my ribs. Breathing requires conscious effort. Every inhale feels like pulling broken glass into my lungs. Four years of waking up at 4 AM, bleeding onto the page, all erased by a three-line template. I bite the inside of my cheek until I taste copper.

The heavy wax seal of the publishing house lay broken on the rug, a deep crimson fracture. Arthur stood by the fireplace, the parchment trembling in his pale, ink-stained hands. "Not quite right for our press," he whispered to the empty study. He fed the letter to the flames, watching the edges curl and blacken, but the destruction brought no relief. The rejection felt like a physical hook lodged deep beneath his ribs, twisting with every breath. He collapsed into his leather armchair, pulling his knees toward his chest. His mind raced back through the thousands of hours spent by candlelight, the drafts, the ruined quills. A low, guttural noise escaped his throat, a sound more animal than human. He squeezed his eyes shut, but the publisher's crest burned brightly in the dark. He wrapped his arms around his head, rocking slowly, unable to escape his own skull.

I sit in the driver's seat with the engine off, my forehead resting against the cold steering wheel. The ping from my dream publisher had sent my heart racing, only for it to plummet into an endless void. Now, the silence of the garage is deafening. My hands grip the leather, squeezing until my wrists shake and my joints pop. I keep hitting rewind on my life, thinking of every dinner I missed, every weekend locked away to write. "The narrative lacks the necessary momentum." The phrase bounces off the windshield and burrows into me like a parasite. I punch the dashboard, once, twice, the hard plastic scraping my knuckles raw. A single tear drops onto my jeans, hot and heavy. I gasp for air, feeling completely hollowed out, as if my internal organs have been forcefully scooped from my chest, leaving only an echoing emptiness.

"Mom, are you okay?" Leo’s small voice pulled Clara back to the sunny kitchen. She was staring at the cutting board, her knife hovering over an apple. On the counter, her laptop displayed the publisher's logo and the words: "While we appreciate the opportunity..." Clara forced a brittle smile, though her jaw ached from clenching. "Just fine, honey." As Leo ran outside, her mask slipped. Clara dropped the knife and gripped the counter, her knuckles stark white. A phantom pressure bore down on her spine, forcing her to hunch over the sink. Her lungs forgot how to expand. The characters she had nurtured for five years felt like corpses, their voices violently silenced by an editor in New York. She pressed a hand over her mouth to stifle a ragged gasp, her shoulders heaving. Every single heartbeat felt like a heavy iron hammer striking an exposed nerve.

The glow of my phone illuminates the ceiling. 3:17 AM. I roll onto my side, tangling the damp sheets around my legs. The editor's words play on a relentless loop behind my eyes. "We didn't connect with the protagonist." I punch my pillow, desperate for a cold side that doesn't exist. My skin feels too tight, crawling with an invisible itch that I scratch at until red lines welt on my forearms. I bled onto those pages. I throw the covers off and pace the tiny gap between the bed and the closet. I bite down on my thumbnail, tearing the cuticle until a drop of blood wells up. The sting grounds me for a second, but then the spinning thoughts restart. My chest tightens, a heavy block of ice settling over my lungs. I drop to my knees, burying my face in the mattress, silently screaming into the dark.

The commuter train rattled over the tracks, but Marcus heard nothing but a dull roaring in his ears. He stared at his phone, the email from his idolized publisher glaring back. His reflection in the dark window showed a man slowly coming apart. He rubbed his face vigorously, as if he could scrub away the rejection, his hands trembling with restless energy. A heavy, sickening dread sloshed in his belly. He wanted to pry open the train doors and step out into the rushing wind. Instead, he simply sat there, gripping his briefcase so tightly the leather groaned. He closed his eyes, and a sharp, pulsing pain shot behind his eyelids. Ten years of hope, casually discarded by a polite form letter. He kept swallowing, trying to dislodge the massive, jagged lump in his throat. He let out a shaky, broken exhale, feeling the narrow carriage walls closing in.

I sit on the park bench, pigeons gathering at my feet. I have nothing to give them. The rejection letter from my dream publisher is folded into a tiny, dense square in my pocket. I press my thumb against it, letting the sharp corners dig into my flesh until it stings. It’s the only way I know I’m not dreaming. My mind is a whirlwind of glass shards, tearing at every memory of writing that book. I can’t breathe right. Every inhale stutters, catching in my throat like I’m breathing through wet sand. I watch a child laugh on the swings, and the bright sound grates against my eardrums, violently out of place in my ruined world. I dig my fingernails into the denim over my thighs, rocking back and forth just an inch, whispering, "It's gone, it's gone," over and over to the empty air.

Sarah dragged the folder labeled 'Final Manuscript' to the trash icon. She hovered the cursor over it, her hand shaking so desperately the mouse clattered against the wood desk. The rejection from Orbit Books burned in her second monitor. "Not the right fit." She slammed her fist onto the keyboard, sending a jumble of meaningless letters across a blank document. She pulled her knees to her chest, her breath coming in rapid, shallow gasps. A cold sweat broke out across her forehead. She felt physically ill, a sharp wave of nausea washing over her as the gravity of the "no" fully settled deep in her bones. Scrambling out of her chair, she paced the room like a caged animal. She clawed at the collar of her shirt, frantically needing more air. The walls of her small home office seemed to warp and bend, mocking her years of wasted labor.

I grip the edges of the bathroom sink, refusing to look up. If I look in the mirror, I’ll see a failure. The polite decline from Vintage Books is burned into my retinas. My chest heaves, but no air seems to reach my lungs. I turn the cold tap on and plunge my hands into the water, splashing it onto my face, but it doesn't wash away the suffocating weight pressing heavily down on my chest. I stare at the drain, watching the water swirl into the dark. My jaw is locked so tight my teeth grind together with a sickening squeak. I want to smash the mirror above me. I want to shatter the glass and feel it bite into my knuckles. Instead, I just slide down the cold porcelain basin, curling into a tight ball on the bathmat. I pull my hair, trying to distract myself from the crushing void.

The bartender set another glass down, but David didn't touch it. He just stared at the amber liquid, seeing the editor's signature floating in the ice. He had promised his wife this publisher would be the one. They had requested the full manuscript. And then, the generic decline. David dug his nails into his thighs under the sticky bar. His stomach churned with a violent mix of dread and sour bile. The clinking glasses around him sounded like a dozen shattering windows. He squeezed his eyes shut, but a sharp ache bloomed behind his temples, radiating down his neck. He wanted to peel his own skin off, to erase the last six years of his life. A ragged, wet breath escaped him, and he buried his face in his calloused hands. He pressed his fingers hard into his eye sockets, wishing the physical pressure would stop the endless, spinning reel of inadequacy.

I don't have an umbrella, but the rain doesn't matter. It soaks through my coat, heavy and freezing, yet the chill cannot rival the ice in my veins. My phone is dead in my pocket. I don't need it. I memorized the rejection email from Knopf within seconds. I walk without a destination, my boots splashing carelessly into deep puddles. Every step feels like dragging iron weights. I clench my jaw until a sharp pain shoots up to my ear. Why did I ever think I was good enough? The voices of doubt, usually just whispers, are now screaming at me, deafening and vicious. I stop under a flickering streetlamp and tilt my head back. I open my mouth to yell, to release the massive, tearing pressure built up in my chest, but no sound comes out. I just stand there, shivering violently, gasping for air in the middle of the flooded intersection.

I zoomed in on the photo she sent, my breath catching in my throat as I recognized the peeling red paint of the diner down my street. My fingers hovered over the keyboard, trembling so hard I dropped my phone onto the mattress. I couldn’t swallow. The sanctuary we had built in our late-night chats felt utterly shattered. She was here. In my city. I paced from the bedroom to the kitchen, digging my nails into my palms until crescent moons of red bloomed on the skin. I wanted to tell her, but the thought of sitting across from her, exposing my physical self, made acid rise in my throat. I stared at the ceiling for hours that night, the screen glowing next to my pillow, a heavy iron weight pressing down on my chest as I typed and deleted my response twenty times.

Elias slammed his laptop shut, the metallic click echoing in his silent apartment. The gamer tag 'CinderOwl' belonged to a barista at the café beneath his office. He pressed the heels of his hands hard into his eye sockets until bursts of color exploded in the darkness. Every morning for a year, he had shared his deepest secrets with CinderOwl. Now, the thought of walking into that café made a cold sweat break out across his forehead. He began taking the fire stairs to the sixth floor, his chest heaving, jumping at the sound of the lobby doors opening. At night, he lay awake, grinding his teeth, imagining the moment she might recognize his voice ordering a black coffee. The safe distance of the internet was gone, leaving him twisting his bedsheets into knots, dreading the morning sun.

"Did you hear those sirens?" The message popped up on my screen, perfectly synced with the wailing fire engine rushing past my window. I yanked the curtains shut, retreating to the darkest corner of my room. My stomach performed a slow, sickening roll. For three years, Marcus was a pixelated icon on the other side of the country—or so I thought. I hugged my knees to my chest, rocking slightly as the reality settled over me. He lived in Seattle. I lived in Seattle. The anonymity that allowed me to be brave was gone. I rubbed my temples, trying to block out the loud thumping of my own heartbeat. I imagined him walking down the avenue, turning a corner, catching sight of my face. The urge to smash my router into pieces fought with the desperate need to keep reading his messages.

When Clara saw the background of the video call, the familiar skyline of Chicago glowing behind him, her throat tightened like a vise. She abruptly ended the call, throwing the webcam into a drawer. For the next three days, she couldn't eat. She flinched every time her phone buzzed, the sound sending electric jolts of panic through her limbs. Her mind played out a hundred disastrous scenarios of bumping into him at the grocery store or the train station. She began wearing oversized sunglasses and a hat when she took the trash out, her gaze darting to every stranger's face. The charming stranger who understood her soul was now a physical threat to her carefully constructed isolation. She sat on the kitchen floor, tugging at the ends of her hair, the unread notification light blinking rhythmically in the dark, mocking her paralysis.

The realization hit me when he complained about the broken escalator at the Montgomery Street station. My fingers froze mid-keystroke. That was my station. I clamped a hand over my mouth, suppressing a dry heave. The sprawling distance between us had been a comforting blanket, and now it was ripped away. I started taking the bus, adding an hour to my commute just to avoid that underground platform. During meetings, I would lose my train of thought, imagining his face in the crowd. I scrubbed my face with cold water, staring into the bathroom mirror until my reflection blurred. How long until he asked to meet? How long until I ruined the perfect illusion I had crafted online? My chest ached with a constant, hollow throb, and I chewed my lower lip until I tasted copper, paralyzed by the blinking cursor on my screen.

Leo stared at the location pin glowing on his phone screen. It was an apartment complex three blocks away. He dropped the device onto the carpet and began pacing the narrow length of his living room, his breathing shallow and rapid. The digital confidant who knew about his greatest failures lived in his neighborhood. Leo ran his hands through his hair, gripping the roots until his scalp burned. He couldn't go to the local bakery anymore. He couldn't walk his dog through the park. Every figure in a winter coat made his heart hammer violently against his ribs. He stood by the window, peeking through the horizontal blinds, entirely consumed by the fear of being perceived. His dinner sat cold on the counter, entirely forgotten, as he watched the streetlights flicker on, trapped in a cage of his own neighborhood.

"Just got back from Miller's Pond," her text read. I stared at the words, the glow of the screen illuminating my trembling hands. Miller's Pond was a five-minute walk from my porch. I squeezed my eyes shut, a heavy knot forming in my throat. The fantasy of our faraway connection shattered, leaving sharp edges behind. I crawled under my duvet, pulling it over my head to block out the world. Every car driving past my house sounded like a threat. What if she walked by? What if she recognized my laugh from our voice notes? My jaw ached from clenching it, and my thoughts spun in dizzying, inescapable circles. I drafted a message saying I was moving to Europe, then deleted it. I typed that I was sick, then backspaced again. I lay there in the dark, suffocated by the sudden, terrifying proximity.

The photo showed a specific mural of a blue whale. Maya recognized the cracked pavement instantly; it was the alley behind her favorite bookstore. She gasped, shoving the phone away as if it had burned her. Her knees grew weak, and she sank onto the edge of her bathtub, resting her forehead against the cool porcelain sink. The man she poured her heart out to on the forums wasn't thousands of miles away. He breathed the same smoggy city air. She wrapped her arms around her stomach, fighting a sudden wave of nausea. For weeks, Maya avoided the downtown area entirely, ordering groceries online, keeping her curtains drawn. She jumped when the floorboards creaked, obsessively checking her locks. The digital sanctuary she cherished had collapsed, leaving her pacing the hallways until dawn, tracing patterns on the wall with cold, shaking fingers.

When he mentioned the awful construction noise on 4th and Elm, the coffee mug slipped from my grasp, shattering against the hardwood floor. I didn’t even flinch at the crash. I just stared at the spreading brown puddle. 4th and Elm was right outside my bedroom window. I sank to my knees, not bothering to avoid the ceramic shards, my breath coming in short, ragged gasps. I had told him things I hadn't told my own mother. He knew my deepest flaws. And he was right outside. I crawled away from the window, pressing my back against the locked door of my closet. The thought of him seeing the real me, the mess I actually was, made my skin crawl with heat. I clutched my phone to my chest, squeezing my eyes shut as the construction drills outside mirrored the frantic pounding in my head.

Oliver read the discord message again. "Going to the indie fest at Centennial Park today." The park was visible from Oliver’s balcony. He stumbled backward, knocking over a stack of books. He couldn't breathe. He grabbed the collar of his shirt, pulling at it as though it were strangling him. His online sanctuary, the only place he felt truly seen, had violently collided with reality. He spent the entire afternoon pacing behind his blackout curtains, his fingernails digging into his palms. Every time he heard a crowd cheering from the park, a fresh wave of ice washed over his spine. He couldn't bring himself to look out the window, yet he couldn't tear his mind away from the festival. He sat in the dark corner of his room, hugging his knees, phone turned off, drowning in a sea of his own racing thoughts.

A picture of a half-eaten pretzel at 'Salty Joe's' popped into our chat. The blood drained from my face. I work at Salty Joe's. I gripped the edge of my kitchen counter until my knuckles turned white, my reflection in the microwave showing wide, terrified eyes. We had joked about meeting someday, but 'someday' was a safe, abstract concept. Now, I scrutinized every customer who walked through the shop doors, my hands shaking so badly I dropped coins while making change. Was the guy in the red beanie him? What about the man in the corner booth? I couldn't eat. I couldn't focus. I spent my breaks locked in the bathroom stall, my head resting against the cold tile, trying to slow my racing heartbeat. The digital wall protecting my fragile reality had crumbled, leaving me exposed to the blinding, terrifying light.

When she casually named the local library branch she frequented, Arthur’s world tilted on its axis. He closed the browser tab, his hands trembling as he pushed away from the desk. He retreated to his bed, curling into a tight ball, his jaw clamped shut. The brilliant woman he debated with every night was reading books in the same building he visited every Sunday. He skipped his weekend trip, staring at the ceiling instead, a profound heaviness anchoring him to the mattress. He imagined her looking up from a novel, recognizing his face from a shared photo, and seeing the quiet, unremarkable man he truly was. The fear tasted like ash in his mouth. He spent the night walking circles in his cramped bedroom, rubbing the back of his neck, unable to type a single word of reply to her glowing green notification.

Elias stared at the glowing screen until his retinas burned. The little blue tick next to Mr. Harrison’s username sat there, mocking him. It was 3:00 AM, and Elias had spent the last four hours scrolling through three years of his own posts, mentally cataloging every expletive, every dumb joke, every late-night rant he had ever typed. He dragged his palms down his face, pressing his fingers into his eye sockets until sparks danced in the darkness. Every time he closed his eyes, he saw Harrison’s expectant, disappointed face at the front of the classroom. His stomach churned, a heavy block of acid rising in his throat. He threw the phone across the mattress, but the silence of his room offered no refuge. He curled his knees to his chest, gripping his hair in tight fists, waiting for a morning he desperately wished would never arrive.

I kept my eyes glued to the woodgrain of my desk, tracing a gouge with a sweaty thumbnail. Mrs. Albright was lecturing about the French Revolution, but her voice sounded like it was coming from underwater. Did she see the photos from Friday night? The question pulsed behind my temples, a relentless drumbeat. Every time she paced past my row, my breath hitched, trapping dead air in my lungs. I dug my nails into my palms, leaving deep crescent-moon indentations. When she paused near my shoulder to emphasize a point about the guillotine, a cold sweat broke out across my collarbones. I imagined her scrolling, pausing, judging. My foot tapped against the metal chair leg—tap, tap, tap—until the girl next to me shot a glare. I couldn't stop. I just wanted to melt through the floorboards and disappear into the dirt below the school.

The notification ping echoed in Maya’s earbuds, making her flinch. "@coach_davis started following you." She dropped her AP Chemistry textbook. It hit the linoleum with a heavy thud, but Maya didn't move to pick it up. Her hands shook violently as she hovered her thumb over the block button, but a chilling thought froze her: What if blocking him makes it worse? She leaned against the cold metal of her locker, sliding down until she hit the floor. The hallway buzzed with passing students, yet she heard nothing but the rush of blood in her ears. She pulled her knees up, wrapping her arms tight around them to stop the tremors. He had seen the poetry she posted on her alternate account. The deeply personal, raw lines. She pressed her face into her kneecaps, wishing her mind would just shut off for one single second.

The espresso machine hissed, but the sound couldn't drown out the buzzing in my head. I stared at the pastry case, counting the muffins, trying to force a normal rhythm back into my breathing. Professor Vance follows you. I had seen the notification five minutes ago, and my chest felt like it was wrapped in barbed wire. My thumb compulsively flicked the edge of my phone case, snapping the plastic back and forth until it finally cracked. I had posted a three-minute rant about his syllabus yesterday. Did he watch it? Did he listen to me mock his monotone voice? I tasted copper and realized I had chewed the inside of my cheek raw. Every time the cafe door chimed, my neck snapped toward the entrance, half-expecting him to walk in. I abandoned my unpaid coffee on the counter and practically bolted out into the street.

Rain lashed against the bus window, matching the chaotic static in Leo’s brain. His screen displayed Mr. Miller’s profile picture. Leo swallowed hard, fighting a wave of intense nausea. He dragged his thumb down, refreshing the page again, hoping the "Follows You" badge was a glitch. It wasn't. He shoved the phone into the deepest pocket of his backpack, but the device felt radioactive. What about the photos from pride last month? The raw, late-night posts he shared? Leo’s breath fogged the cold glass. He rubbed at his chest, trying to massage away the suffocating knot lodged behind his ribs. He couldn't face history class tomorrow. He just couldn't. He closed his eyes, gripping the handrail in front of him so tightly his knuckles turned completely white, quietly praying the bus would just keep driving past his stop and never turn back.

"Pass the peas, please," my mother said, but her voice sounded lightyears away. I pushed the food around my plate, my stomach in rigid, painful knots. My phone sat face-down next to my water glass. It felt like a ticking bomb. Señora Cortez is following your account. I had spent the last hour meticulously deleting hundreds of posts, my heart hammering against my ribs the entire time. Why was she looking at my page? I squeezed my eyes shut, replaying the last six months of my online life. The skipped classes I bragged about. The complaints about her assignments. "Are you feeling alright, sweetie?" my dad asked. I jumped, my fork clattering loudly against the porcelain plate. "Fine," I choked out, though my hands were clammy and my pulse was roaring in my ears. I excused myself, bolted upstairs, and threw up in the bathroom sink.

Chloe’s paintbrush snapped cleanly in two. She stared at the jagged wooden splinters in her palm, unblinking. On the table nearby, her iPad screen remained illuminated on Mrs. Gable’s Instagram page. The notification had popped up mid-stroke, and now, the vibrant canvas before Chloe looked entirely gray. The studio, usually her sanctuary, felt like a shrinking box. Gable had seen the sketches. The dark, cynical caricatures of the school faculty, including Gable herself with exaggerated, monstrous features. Chloe paced the length of the room, her boots scuffing the hardwood. She pulled at the collar of her shirt, gasping as if the air had suddenly thinned out. She grabbed a rag and furiously scrubbed at a perfectly dry palette, her movements erratic and harsh. The silence of the empty studio pressed down on her shoulders, a crushing, physical weight she couldn't throw off.

I ran until my lungs burned, but I couldn't outpace the image of my phone screen. Coach Henderson wants to follow you. I hit the third mile marker and pushed harder, sprinting until my legs felt like lead. The rhythmic pounding of my sneakers did nothing to quiet the frantic shouting in my mind. He saw my weekend stories. He saw the red solo cups, the blurry basement parties, the curfew I broke on Friday. I stumbled onto the grass and collapsed, gasping for air, clutching my head in both hands. Sweat stung my eyes, blurring the stadium lights above into harsh, glaring halos. I imagined him benching me for the season. I imagined the disappointed talks. I dug my fingers into the damp earth, tearing up handfuls of grass from the roots, desperate for a way to rewind time just twenty-four hours.

Tariq sat in the back corner of the university library, surrounded by towering stacks, yet feeling completely exposed. He stared at the screen. Dr. Aris, his thesis advisor, had just retweeted his anonymous vent account. Tariq’s jaw clenched so hard his teeth ached. He repeatedly pressed the backspace key, deleting and retyping the same sentence of his essay without reading a word. His leg bounced in a frantic, ceaseless rhythm, rattling the heavy oak table. Every shadow that shifted at the edge of the bookshelves made his shoulders flinch. He had poured his darkest, most cynical thoughts into that account, masking his identity, or so he thought. He squeezed his eyes shut, pressing the heels of his hands fiercely against his temples, trying to crush the endless loop of worst-case scenarios currently playing out in his racing mind.

The pavement cracked beneath my boots, but I barely registered the cold wind slapping my face. I couldn't stop looking over my shoulder. Mr. Finch follows you. The notification popped up right as the final bell rang. I shoved my phone into my pocket, but it felt like a branding iron against my thigh. Why my private account? How did he find it? I crossed the street without checking for cars, a horn blaring loudly, but I just kept walking, my vision narrowing to a tunnel. I gnawed on my lower lip until I tasted blood. He knew about my family's struggles now. He knew about the days I pretended to be sick. I stopped under a flickering streetlamp, burying my face in my cold, trembling hands, glued to the pavement, unable to take another step forward or backward.

Jenna fumbled the stack of folded sweaters, sending them tumbling to the retail floor. She dropped to her knees, but her hands hovered uselessly over the garments. From her apron pocket, her phone vibrated—another like from Mrs. Vance. Jenna’s throat tightened, restricting her airway until she was taking short, shallow gasps. She had called in sick to Vance's seminar yesterday, claiming a high fever. Later that night, she posted videos from a loud concert downtown. Jenna grabbed a sweater, twisting the fabric between her fists as if trying to strangle it. The store’s upbeat pop music felt like a physical assault on her senses. She scrambled to her feet, abandoning the mess, and pushed through the doors of the employee breakroom. She collapsed into a plastic chair, pulling her knees to her chest, rocking back and forth as hot tears spilled down her cheeks.

The cafeteria hummed with hundreds of voices, but I sat at the edge of the table entirely isolated in my own head. I kept unlocking my phone, staring at the little icon next to Dr. Brooks’s name, then locking it again. My half-eaten sandwich sat like a brick in my stomach. Every laugh from the table over sounded like a mockery. I scrubbed my hands vigorously over my face, trying to erase the phantom feeling of his eyes on me. I had shared an article heavily criticizing his published research just two days ago. Did he see my snarky caption? My leg jittered so hard it shook the table, spilling a drop of Liam's soda. "Dude, chill," Liam muttered, but I couldn't. I bolted up, grabbing my tray, desperately needing to be anywhere but under the invisible, crushing microscope that suddenly trapped me.

I stare at the ceiling, tracing the cracks in the plaster until my eyes burn. The email is still open on my laptop, glowing in the dark room. Correction: The Carter Grant was awarded in error. The intended recipient is Michael Vance. Michael is sleeping in the bunk above me. His soft snores sound like accusations. I grip the edges of my mattress, my knuckles aching. If I tell the financial aid office, I pack my bags tomorrow. If I don’t, I spend every day looking at the guy whose life I stole. My stomach churns, acid rising in my throat. I roll over, pressing my palms against my ears to block out the silence of the room, but the pounding of my own heart just gets louder. Tomorrow, he’ll ask me why I look so exhausted, and I’ll have to smile and lie again.

Elias stirred his coffee until it spilled over the rim, staining his thesis notes. The congratulations banner hanging in the cafe seemed to mock him. In his pocket, the crumpled letter felt heavier than a stone. Due to a clerical error involving matching surnames... He looked across the quad and saw Chloe Elias, the brilliant girl who spent every waking hour in the lab, sitting on a bench eating a stale bagel. He had cashed the check yesterday. His mother had cried tears of joy on the phone, telling him she could finally sleep. Elias dug his fingernails into his thighs under the table, his breath coming in shallow, ragged gasps. Every time he tried to stand up and walk over to Chloe, his legs locked. He sat there for hours, the cold coffee pooling around his papers, a prisoner in his own skin.

The linoleum floor of the administrative building squeaks beneath my sneakers. I’ve paced this exact hallway twenty times in the last hour. My hand hovers over the brass doorknob of the bursar’s office, shaking so badly I can hear my wristwatch rattling. Dear Ms. Greene, please disregard the previous correspondence. It was meant for a Sarah Green, no 'e'. Just one letter different. I press my forehead against the cool painted wall, closing my eyes, but all I see is my dad’s proud smile when I told him he wouldn't have to take a second mortgage. A bitter taste floods my mouth. I walk away from the door, then stop at the stairs, pivot, and walk back. My chest feels wrapped in barbed wire. I reach for the knob again, my breath hitching, trapped perfectly between ruining my family and ruining a stranger.

Maya sat shivering in the darkest corner of the library stacks, her knees pulled tightly to her chest. The notification on her phone remained unread, but she already knew what the preview text said. She rocked back and forth, her teeth clamped down on her lower lip until the metallic taste of blood coated her tongue. The university had sent her the conservatory funding meant for the other cellist. She had already bought the antique bow. She had already played it at the recital. Every scrape of a chair from the floor above made her flinch, imagining the dean coming to demand it all back. She squeezed her eyes shut, trying to block out the phantom sound of applause that now sounded like mocking laughter. Maya dug her fingers into her own hair, pulling sharply, desperate for a physical pain to drown out the noise in her head.

"To our little scholar," my father booms, raising his glass of cheap champagne. My mother beams, her eyes wet. I force the corners of my mouth up, lifting my own glass, though my hand trembles so violently the liquid sloshes over the edge. I can’t swallow the roast chicken; it feels like ash in my throat. Just three hours ago, I saw the true recipient's name buried in the forwarded email chain. J. Harrison, not J. Harris. I excuse myself and lock the bathroom door, bracing both hands on the porcelain sink. I stare at my reflection, hating the face looking back at me. I turn the faucet on full blast to drown out the sound of my parents laughing in the dining room. I slide down the wall, pulling my knees up, burying my face in my hands as hot tears soak into my jeans.

Paint dripped from Liam’s brush onto the hardwood floor, a steady rhythm that mirrored his racing pulse. The gallery had funded his portfolio by mistake—the acceptance letter he’d framed on his wall explicitly mentioned the bronze sculptures, which were entirely the work of his roommate, David. Liam stared at his own canvas. It looked hollow, amateurish. He could hear David in the next room, quietly packing a suitcase to move back to his parents' farm because he couldn't afford tuition. Liam’s jaw ached from grinding his teeth. He picked up a palette knife, his knuckles white, and slashed a jagged line right through the center of his painting. He dragged the blade down again and again, ripping the canvas to shreds, panting heavily, unable to stop until there was nothing left but empty wooden stretcher bars and the sound of David’s zipper closing next door.

The tailor pins the hem of my graduation robe, humming cheerfully. I stare straight ahead at the mirror, but my vision is blurred. The bursar’s apology letter is folded into a tiny, sharp square in my pocket, pressing into my hip like a dagger. The full ride for the study abroad program was a clerical mix-up. It belonged to the girl standing three feet away from me, getting her own gown fitted. She is on the phone, telling her mother she has to work double shifts all summer to pay off her loans. Every word she speaks feels like a physical blow to my ribs. I swallow hard, fighting a sudden wave of nausea. I want to rip the black robe off my shoulders. I want to scream the truth. Instead, I just stand there, completely rigid, letting the tailor stitch me into a lie.

Snow crunched beneath Priya’s boots, but she couldn’t feel the cold. She hadn't slept in four days. The shadows under her eyes were dark bruises. The STEM grant was supposed to go to a graduate student named Peter, but a database glitch had deposited the fifty thousand dollars into her account. She stopped in the middle of the bridge, watching the icy river rush below. Her hands gripped the frozen iron railing. She had already wired half the money to her grandmother for surgery. There was no way to get it back. Priya squeezed her eyes closed, seeing Peter’s face from the department meeting—he had looked so defeated, so exhausted. A sharp gasp tore from her throat. She hit her forehead against the icy metal of the railing, once, twice, wishing the cold could numb the crushing weight sitting square in the center of her chest.

The rhythmic clack of the train tracks usually puts me to sleep, but today every jolt sends a fresh rush of adrenaline through my veins. I stare out the window at the blurred trees, my reflection superimposed over the passing world. The athletic department's letter burns in my backpack. We apologize for the miscommunication; the diving scholarship was awarded to Aaron Miller. But I've already signed the lease. I've already bought the gear. I bite the inside of my cheek until I taste copper. Aaron had a torn ACL; this was his only way into college. My leg starts bouncing on its own, a frantic, uncontrollable tremor. The woman next to me shoots me an irritated look. I apologize, my voice cracking, and grip my knee to force it still. I close my eyes, but the darkness just makes the twisting knot in my stomach tighter.

Samir sat alone in the dark newsroom, the glow of the monitor illuminating the sweat on his forehead. The expose he was writing about the university's corrupt financial aid system sat unfinished. On his desk was a private memo he had unearthed during his investigation—a memo detailing how his own prestigious journalism fellowship was a typo. It was meant for his rival, Jenna. Samir’s fingers hovered over the keyboard, shaking. He typed a sentence, then immediately held down the backspace key. He stood up, knocking his chair backward with a loud clatter. He paced to the window, ran both hands aggressively through his hair, and let out a long, ragged exhale. Jenna had dropped out yesterday. Samir picked up his coffee mug and hurled it at the brick wall, watching it shatter into dozens of jagged pieces, wishing the noise would quiet his own mind.

I feed the pigeons aggressively, throwing handfuls of breadcrumbs so hard the birds scatter. The crisp autumn air does nothing to cool the flush creeping up my neck. The phone in my pocket vibrates again. It’s the dean’s office. I don’t answer. I know what they want. They realized I’m the wrong Alex. The right Alex is a single mom taking night classes. I grip the edge of the wooden bench, my fingernails digging into the peeling green paint until splinters lodge under my skin. I welcome the sting. It distracts me from the image of my own empty bank account and the eviction notice on my apartment door. I draw my knees to my chest and press the heels of my hands against my eyes. Sparks of light burst in my vision as I rock forward, unable to breathe, caught in a trap I didn’t set.

The clock on the wall ticked loud enough to echo. Three a.m. Marcus lay rigid on his back, the heavy comforter feeling like a lead vest. The email from the engineering department was etched into the back of his eyelids. He hadn't meant to open the attached spreadsheet, but now he knew his full-tuition award was actually meant for the international student down the hall. Marcus heard footsteps shuffling in the corridor, followed by the soft click of a door. Was that him? Was he awake, trying to figure out how to pay his tuition? Marcus grabbed his pillow and jammed it over his face, pressing down hard as if he could suffocate his own thoughts. His chest heaved against the mattress. He curled into a tight fetal position, his muscles cramping from tension, waiting for a morning that he desperately wished would never arrive.

Elias sat on the edge of his unmade bed, his laptop screen glowing with a damning red 85% match. He traced the highlighted lines, the exact phrasing from a journal article he swore he’d never read. His fingers dug into his scalp, pulling at the roots of his hair until his eyes watered. Every time he closed his eyes, Professor Vance’s cold, disappointed stare materialized in the darkness. "We take academic integrity seriously, Elias." The words echoed in his skull, loud as a blaring siren. He hadn't eaten in two days. The half-eaten sandwich on his desk smelled like ash. He stood up, paced to the window, and pressed his burning forehead against the cold glass, his chest tight as if wrapped in iron bands. He opened his mouth to take a deep breath, but the air simply wouldn't fill his lungs.

I sit in the stiff wooden chair outside the disciplinary office, my knee bouncing so violently it shakes the entire row of seats. I stare at my fingernails, chewed down past the quick, bleeding slightly at the edges. I don't feel the sting. All I hear is the deafening tick-tock of the wall clock. Tick. Expulsion. Tock. Ruined career. I didn't copy that code; I wrote it at 3 AM fueled by black coffee and desperation. But the timestamp on the repository says otherwise. A harsh cramp twists my stomach, sending a wave of sour nausea up my throat. I fold myself in half, pressing my forehead against my knees, trying to block out the fluorescent lights buzzing above me like angry hornets. If I could just unzip my skin and step out of this body, leaving the accusation behind, I would do it in a heartbeat.

The towering library stacks felt like a closing vice around Sarah. She dumped her backpack onto the oak table, frantically pulling out notebooks, loose sticky notes, and printed PDFs. She needed to find her original drafts. She had to. Her hands shook violently, sending a flurry of papers cascading onto the carpet. She dropped to her knees, scrambling to gather them, her vision blurring with hot tears. "Please, please, please," she whispered to the empty aisle, the sound fracturing in her throat. She flipped through a green spiral notebook, but the pages were blank. Where were the outlines? Did she type them on the library computer? She clamped her hands over her ears, trying to muffle the relentless internal voice screaming that no one would believe her. A heavy sob ripped through her chest, leaving her gasping for air on the dusty floor.

The rain soaks through my jacket, but I keep walking, dragging my boots through the deep puddles along the sidewalk. The notification from the academic integrity board is a phantom weight vibrating in my pocket. I pull my phone out again, staring at the blurry screen until the black text burns into my retinas. Subject: Notice of Plagiarism Investigation. I press the heel of my palm hard against my sternum, trying to massage away the crushing weight sitting right over my heart. I wrote every single word of that essay. I poured weeks of research into it. Yet, somehow, the algorithm flagged it as generated. I scream into the empty street, a raw, ragged sound that scratches my throat. I kick a trash can, sending it clattering onto the asphalt, then immediately sink against the wet brick wall, burying my face in my damp hands.

The dining hall was a cacophony of clinking silverware and overlapping laughter, but Marcus sat in a bubble of deafening silence. His roommate was telling a joke, waving a fork in the air, but Marcus only saw the motion in a detached slow motion. "He stole it. He bought it online." That's what Dr. Aris had declared this morning. Marcus pushed a cold piece of chicken around his plate, his stomach performing sick, violent rolls. He felt a bead of sweat drip down the back of his neck despite the blasting air conditioning. He dug his nails into his thighs under the table, pressing until the pain grounded him for a fraction of a second. Every glance from a passing student felt like a physical strike. They knew. He was convinced they all knew. He abruptly stood, knocking his chair backward with a loud clatter, and fled the room.

The glowing red numbers of my digital clock mock me: 4:13 AM. This is the third night in a row I haven’t slept. I roll onto my side, then my back, tangling the damp sheets around my legs in a suffocating knot. The dean’s voice plays on a relentless, inescapable loop in my head: "The similarities to the published thesis are statistically impossible to ignore." I squeeze my eyes shut, pressing my fists hard against my eyelids until explosions of color burst in the dark. I didn't steal the design. I don't even know who that author is. I throw off the covers and pace the length of my tiny room, taking exactly six steps each way. Back and forth. Six steps. Turn. Six steps. My chest heaves with shallow, insufficient breaths. I just want the looping thoughts to stop. I just want one minute of silence.

The lecture hall emptied out, leaving Chloe standing alone at the front podium. Professor Lin didn't look up from packing his briefcase. "My decision stands, Chloe. The committee will review your assignment." Chloe’s jaw trembled so hard her teeth clicked together. She gripped the edges of the wooden podium, her knuckles turning bone-white. "But I have the version history," she choked out, her voice cracking into a pathetic squeak. "I can show you the timestamps." Professor Lin zipped his bag and walked past her without another word. Chloe’s knees gave out the moment the heavy door clicked shut behind him. She collapsed into the front row seat, wrapping her arms tightly around her stomach as if trying to hold her organs inside. She rocked back and forth, a low, guttural whimper escaping her lips as the walls of the classroom seemed to tilt and close in on her.

I hold the phone a few inches away from my ear, listening to my mother cheerfully discuss her plans for my graduation party. "We booked the caterer," she says, her voice full of pride. I bite down on my lower lip so hard I taste copper. A sickening wave of vertigo hits me, forcing me to grip the kitchen counter to stay upright. The plagiarism hearing is tomorrow morning. There might not be a graduation. "That sounds great, Mom," I force out, my voice sounding hollow and metallic to my own ears. I hang up and immediately slide down the cabinet doors until I hit the linoleum floor. I pull my knees to my chest and bury my face in them. My breathing hitches in erratic gasps. I imagine the look on her face when she finds out I’ve been expelled for cheating. The image physically burns my chest.

Paint splattered across the canvas in jagged, angry strokes as Leo violently dragged his brush over his final project. The printed note from his studio instructor lay crumpled on the floor, accusing him of tracing a digital artist's composition. He hadn't. It was his own reference photo. Leo threw the brush across the room; it smacked against the brick wall, leaving a red streak resembling a fresh wound. He stared at his hands, slick with linseed oil and cadmium red, and began to aggressively scrub them with a rough rag. He scrubbed until his skin was raw, bright pink, and burning, but he couldn't wash away the feeling of being utterly tainted. He sank to the floor amidst the sharp smell of turpentine, pulling his knees up and wrapping his arms around his head, desperately trying to block out the imagined whispers of his peers.

I stare at the blinking cursor on my laptop screen, completely paralyzed. I need to write a new essay for my history class, but my hands refuse to touch the keyboard. Every word that forms in my mind feels like a trap. Is this my thought? Did I read this somewhere? I quickly delete the half-formed sentence, my heart hammering a frantic, uneven rhythm against my ribs. I look around the crowded coffee shop. The barista is glancing my way. The girl at the next table is typing furiously. Do they know? Are they whispering about the girl who stole a literature paper? I grab my mug of green tea, but my hands are shaking so badly the hot liquid sloshes over the rim, scalding my knuckles. I don't even flinch. I just stare at the spilled tea, feeling a heavy, dark cloud pressing down on the base of my skull.

The sunlight on the campus quad was blindingly bright, a harsh contrast to the cold dread hollowed out inside Julian. He had just walked out of the department chair’s office. Zero on the final. Academic probation. All for an uncredited citation he completely forgot to include. Julian stood frozen by the bronze statue of the university founder, his backpack slipping off his shoulder to hit the grass with a dull thud. Students rushed past him in a blur of colors, their voices melting into a distorted, echoing hum. He reached up and tightly gripped handfuls of his own curly hair, pulling downward as if trying to anchor himself to gravity. His chest seized, taking in rapid, shallow gulps of air that did nothing to fill his lungs. He wanted to peel off his own skin. He wanted the earth to split open and swallow him whole.

I run the plagiarism checker for the fifteenth time. The progress bar crawls across the screen, mocking my fraying sanity. The glowing monitor illuminates the empty, dark computer lab. When the result flashes—12% Match—I flinch as if I’ve been slapped. I open the document and frantically delete the flagged paragraph. My vision swims, the black letters blurring into crawling insects on a white wall. I haven't showered in days; I can smell stale sweat and fear radiating off my own clothes. The professor called my integrity a "thin veil of lies" during office hours. The insult echoes in my ears, accompanied by a high-pitched ringing that won't stop. I rest my forehead on the hard edge of the desk, letting the sharp plastic bite into my skin. I squeeze my eyes shut, a single, hot tear slipping out to land on the spacebar with a quiet tap.

I have read the single line of the email forty-seven times, hoping the pixels will somehow rearrange themselves. *We regret to inform you.* My nails dig into the meat of my palms, leaving deep crescent moons that throb in time with the pounding behind my eyes. If I look away from the screen, the reality of the massive tuition bill will close my windpipe. I pace the three feet of floor space between my unmade bed and the scratched desk, a trapped animal with nowhere left to run. Every time I close my eyes, I see my mother picking up a third shift at the diner, her tired spine bending a little further toward the floor. A dry, ragged gasp rips out of my throat. I grab the edge of the desk, knuckles bone-white, desperately trying to stop the room from violently tilting beneath my feet.

The lively chatter of the campus café morphed into a wall of white noise the moment Elias opened the portal. *Status: Unsuccessful.* He stared at the red text until his vision blurred, a cold sweat breaking out across the back of his neck. His hands shook so violently that his coffee spilled, dark liquid staining his meticulously organized chemistry notes. He didn't wipe it up. The buzzing neon sign in the window felt like a strobe light flashing directly into his skull. *How do I tell them?* The thought looped relentlessly, a heavy stone grinding against his ribs. He imagined his father selling the family car, his little sister giving up gymnastics. Elias pressed the heels of his hands hard against his eye sockets until bursts of color exploded in the darkness. He couldn't breathe. The air in the coffee shop had turned to thick, choking ash.

The rhythmic clacking of the train wheels sounds exactly like a ticking clock, counting down the days until I have to drop out. The glossy university crest on the rejection letter burns a hole through my backpack, radiating a heat I can feel against my spine. I press my forehead against the cold, greasy window of the subway car, letting the harsh vibrations rattle my teeth. It’s not enough to drown out the echo of the polite dismissal in my head. *There were many qualified applicants.* I bite the inside of my cheek until I taste copper, swallowing the sharp tang along with the rising bile. Every passenger laughing, every beat leaking from a stranger's headphones, feels like sandpaper scraping across raw nerves. I wrap my arms tight around my stomach, doubling over as invisible claws twist my insides into suffocating, unyielding knots.

Books were stacked like barricades around Clara's desk in the subterranean level of the library, offering no protection against the thin sheet of paper in her trembling hands. The denial letter had arrived in the evening mail. She read the first sentence, stopped, and read it again, a phantom grip wrapping tightly around her throat. She pulled her knees to her chest, rocking slightly in the wooden chair. A harsh, jagged breath hitched in her chest, refusing to go down or come out. The fluorescent lights hummed a cruel, monotonous tune, vibrating directly into the center of her brain. Her fingers twisted violently into her own hair, pulling the roots until her scalp burned, needing a physical sensation to anchor her against the free-fall opening in her stomach. Tomorrow the payment deadline would strike, a blade waiting to sever her from the only future she had ever planned.

I don’t feel the freezing rain soaking through my thin jacket, nor the puddles seeping into my worn sneakers. All I feel is the phantom vibration of my phone, the ghost of the notification that shattered my world ten minutes ago. *The committee has made its final decision.* My chest heaves with dry, shuddering gasps. I lean heavily against a brick alley wall, scraping my shoulder, desperate for the rough texture to ground me. Every shadow stretching across the wet pavement looks like a locked door. I replay the interview over and over, dissecting every stutter and misplaced smile, a relentless loop playing at maximum volume. If I scream, the sound will get swallowed by the storm, but the pressure behind my ribs is expanding, cracking my bones from the inside out, leaving me gasping for a breath that refuses to fill my lungs.

The smell of roasting garlic usually brought Marcus comfort, but tonight, the aroma of his mother’s cooking made his stomach churn violently. He had checked the scholarship portal in the bathroom. *Not selected.* He stared blindly at the chipped formica table, his jaw clenched so tightly his teeth ground in a faint, sickening rhythm. "Set the plates, sweetheart?" his mother called from the stove, her voice dripping with an exhausted pride that felt like acid eating through his skin. Marcus stood, his legs completely numb. He gripped the back of the wooden chair, his knuckles turning a stark, bloodless white. Every second he delayed telling her the truth felt like a physical blow to his abdomen. The brightly lit kitchen walls seemed to shrink, pressing inward, squeezing the oxygen out of the room until his vision edged in a crawling, static darkness.

My charcoal snaps, the brittle stick exploding into dust against the canvas. I stare at the ruined sketch, but all I see is the polite, generic refusal from the merit board. I rub the soot into my jeans, then scrub my hands over my face, leaving dark, messy streaks across my cheeks. My heart is beating a frantic, erratic tempo against my ribs, a trapped bird slamming into a window over and over. Without the funding, I can't afford the supplies for my senior showcase. I pace the length of the empty studio, kicking a stray stool so hard the impact sends a shockwave up my leg. The sharp sting is a welcome distraction from the suffocating dread settling like a lead weight on my chest. I sink to the paint-splattered floor, pulling my knees up, burying my face in my soot-stained hands as the deafening silence of the room crushes me.

The dashboard clock flashed 2:14 AM. Chloe hadn't turned the key in the ignition for over an hour. The glow of her phone illuminated her pale, tear-streaked face, the screen frozen on the financial aid department’s final verdict. She violently threw the phone into the passenger seat, immediately regretting it, then snatched it back, staring at the words again as if pure willpower could rewrite them. Her breathing came in short, jagged hiccups. She slammed her palms against the steering wheel—once, twice, three times—until her skin was bruised and stinging. "No, no, no," she whispered, the words tumbling out in a frantic, broken rhythm. She pressed her forehead against the cold leather of the wheel, her shoulders shaking uncontrollably. The streetlights outside cast long, skeletal shadows across the windshield, resembling prison bars locking her inside a future she could no longer afford.

The ticking of the waiting room clock drives needles into my eardrums. I hold the printed rejection letter on my lap, smoothing the creases until the paper is worn soft, though the words *We cannot offer you an award at this time* remain stark and black. My knee bounces at a frantic pace, shaking the entire row of connected plastic chairs. I aggressively chew on my thumbnail, tasting blood but unable to stop the compulsion. When Mr. Harrison opens his door and smiles at me, asking for the good news, a profound nausea washes into my throat. I try to force a response, but my jaw locks tight. The walls of the tiny counseling center warp and stretch in my peripheral vision. I clutch the crinkled letter to my chest, curling inward, desperately wishing the worn carpet would open up and swallow me whole.

Sweat dripped from Jamal’s nose, pooling on the cracked tiles between his cleats. The athletic director's email was still open on the tablet resting inside his locker. He gripped the edges of the locker door so hard the metal dug deeply into his calloused fingers. His chest rose and fell in rapid, shallow jerks, entirely unrelated to the grueling two-hour soccer practice he had just finished. The locker room was empty, but he could hear the ghostly echoes of his parents bragging to the neighbors about his full ride. He squeezed his eyes shut, pressing his palms to his temples, trying to physically crush the memory out of his skull. A low, ragged moan vibrated in his throat, a sound of profound defeat. He violently kicked his gear bag across the room, watching it hit the wall as his dreams of a university education shattered into heavy, jagged pieces.

My roommate's laughter from the next room feels like shards of glass slipping under my skin. I sit in the dark on our frayed sofa, my laptop screen casting a sickly blue glow over my trembling hands. *After careful consideration.* The phrase repeats in my brain, a skipping record I cannot silence. I wrap my arms around my torso, digging my fingertips into my sides until they ache, trying to hold myself together while everything inside me violently tears apart. My throat feels thick, making every swallow a grueling chore. I bite down on my lower lip, tasting salt and iron, refusing to let the sob claw its way out of my mouth. If I make a sound, it makes it real. I rock back and forth, staring at the peeling wallpaper, paralyzed by the colossal weight of a debt I will never outrun.

The cardboard boxes in the stockroom towered over Maya, but she barely registered the clutter. The scholarship letter was crushed into a damp ball in her apron pocket. She had sneaked away from the register to read it, and now she couldn't force her legs to carry her back to the sales floor. Her breathing hitched, coming in dizzying spurts that made the fluorescent lights swim. She crouched behind a pallet of winter coats, hiding her face against her knees. Her fingers compulsively shredded the edge of her nametag, the plastic snapping beneath her nails. Every time the bell above the store entrance chimed, a fresh wave of nausea rolled through her stomach. She pictured her minimum wage paycheck, stacking the pennies against the towering university fees. A strangled, dry heave shook her shoulders, her hands flying to her mouth to stifle the desperate sound.

David stared at the printed email, the stark black font blurring as a ringing filled his ears. Three years of isolating protein structures. Three years of Dr. Aris guiding his hands. Now, a transfer to Stanford. David’s fingers curled into his palms, nails digging crescents into his flesh until the skin broke. He paced the narrow cold lab, breathing in shallow, erratic gasps, bumping into the centrifuge and ignoring the sharp pain in his hip. He read the words again. *Leaving in December.* The walls of the windowless basement lab seemed to shrink, pressing inward. He grabbed a stack of plastic pipettes and hurled them against the sink, watching them scatter across the tiles. Dropping to his knees, he pressed the heels of his hands violently into his eye sockets, seeing jagged flashes of light, desperate to blot out the crushing weight of a half-finished dissertation that now chained him to the floor.

"I've accepted a position in London," Professor Higgins said softly. The teacup in my hand rattled against its saucer, a violent chatter I couldn't stop. I set it down so hard hot Earl Grey splashed over my knuckles, but I barely registered the burn. London. My breath hitched, caught behind a jagged lump in my throat. I squeezed my eyes shut, but the last four chapters of my thesis flashed behind my eyelids—pages soaked in his red ink. My stomach twisted into a sickening knot. I nodded mechanically, but beneath the desk, I gripped the fabric of my jeans, twisting it until my knuckles turned stark white. The air in the book-lined office abruptly thinned. I wanted to scream, to flip the mahogany desk, to beg him to stay. Instead, I just sat there, gasping against an invisible, crushing weight, while the ticking of his grandfather clock struck my eardrums like a heavy iron hammer.

The campus newsletter slipped from Elena’s trembling fingers, fluttering to the coffee shop floor. *Dr. Vance - Farewell.* She shoved her chair back with a screech that turned the heads of several patrons. She stumbled out the glass doors into the freezing rain, dragging air into her lungs like a drowning woman. Two years of field research, entirely funded by Vance’s grants. She leaned heavily against the wet brick wall of the alley, sliding down until the damp pavement soaked through her coat. She gripped her own hair, pulling the strands hard enough to sting her scalp. Thoughts collided in a chaotic rush: *Who will sign the approvals? Will I have to start over?* A harsh, dry sob tore out of her throat. She rocked back and forth on her heels in the downpour, wrapping her arms tightly around her knees, trying to hold her splintering world together.

Dr. Lin’s voice crackled through my laptop speakers. "They made an offer I couldn't refuse." I stared at his pixelated image, my jaw clamped so tightly my teeth ached. I pressed my thumbnail into the wooden edge of my desk, pushing until a splinter buried itself deeply under the nail. I didn't pull it out. My mind raced in frantic, jagged circles. *The Berlin archives. The methodology. It's all useless now.* "We'll find you a new chair," he added, his tone entirely too casual. I bit down on my lower lip, tasting a sudden, sharp metallic tang as blood flooded my tongue. I slammed the mute button. My chest rose and fell in rapid, shallow jerks. I scratched frantically at my collarbone, leaving angry red welts in my skin. The blinking cursor on my open document mocked me, pulsing like a failing heartbeat while the room tilted dangerously around my chair.

Marcus froze outside the faculty lounge. Through the ajar door, he heard Dr. Thorne laughing. *“Yes, the move to MIT is finalized for January.”* Marcus backed away, his boots silent on the linoleum. He ducked into the empty stairwell and collapsed onto the concrete landing. MIT. January. That was a month before his defense. He buried his face in his hands, pressing his palms into his eyes until geometric sparks exploded. A cold sweat broke out across his forehead. He dry-heaved over his knees, coughing violently. He dragged his nails down his own cheeks, feeling the rough scrape of skin. *Four years.* He whispered it to the empty stairwell, rocking slightly. *Four years.* Every equation, every late-night edit, now tethered to a phantom. He clutched his chest, grabbing a fistful of his sweater as if he could literally massage his furiously hammering heart to slow down.

I sat in the silent reading room, the glowing email reflecting in my glasses. *I will be transitioning to a private think tank at the end of the term.* The silence of the library pressed against my eardrums, turning into a deafening roar. I reached for the stack of index cards I had meticulously color-coded over the last six months. My hands shook so violently that several scattered to the floor. I grabbed a handful—my primary sources, my theoretical frameworks—and tore them straight down the middle. The thick paper resisted, tearing at my cuticles, but I ripped them again. And again. Shards of paper rained onto my lap. I clamped a hand over my mouth to stifle the raw sound clawing its way up my windpipe. I pressed my forehead hard against the cold oak table, screwing my eyes shut as hot, uninvited tears tracked across my nose.

The crosswalk signal flashed a red hand, but Chloe stepped off the curb anyway. Horns blared. A cab swerved, splashing dirty slush against her jeans, but she didn’t flinch. She just kept walking, her gaze fixed blindly on the gray skyline. Professor Ahmadi was leaving. The words echoed in her skull on an endless, chaotic loop, a drumbeat matching her erratic pulse. She shoved her bare hands into her coat pockets, curling her fingers into tight, white-knuckled fists. The cold wind whipped her hair across her face, stinging her eyes, but she didn't brush it away. Her throat felt tight, stuffed with cotton and broken glass. She stopped in the middle of the sidewalk, commuters flowing around her. She squeezed her temples with both hands, pushing hard against the bone, trying desperately to crush the echoing realization that her entire doctoral project was dead in the water.

The heavy wooden door clicked shut, leaving me alone with the whiteboard. *Leaving. Sabbatical turned permanent.* I stared at the complex diagrams we had drawn together just an hour ago, the blue and black marker lines blurring into a chaotic web. My knees gave out. I hit the thin carpet hard, but didn't bother to get up. I crawled toward the wall, pressing my back against the rough cinderblocks. My lungs refused to expand. I gasped for air, sounding like a fish thrown onto dry land, but oxygen wouldn't come. I grabbed the collar of my t-shirt and yanked hard, tearing the seam, needing the fabric away from my throat. I squeezed my knees to my chest and dug my fingers into my own calves until the muscles cramped. My thesis was a house of cards, and she had just casually flicked away the bottom row.

"Just put those journals in the second box, Liam," Dr. Rostova said brightly. Liam nodded, picking up a stack of bound publications. His hands trembled, causing the slick covers to slide against each other. He shoved them into the cardboard box, gripping the fluted edges until the cardboard buckled under his thumbs. She was humming. *Humming.* He gritted his teeth, the muscles in his jaw bunching and popping. A dull ache throbbed behind his eyes, radiating down his neck. He turned away, pretending to examine a framed diploma, just so she wouldn’t see the wild, hunted look painted across his face. His stomach churned violently, a rolling wave of nausea making him swallow hard against bile. He squeezed his eyes shut, his mind flashing to his half-written dissertation. He clamped his hands over his ears for a brief second, desperate to block out the cheerful sound of packing tape.

The clock flashed 3:14 AM in glaring red numbers. I kicked the damp sheets off my legs and rolled over for the hundredth time. Every time I closed my eyes, Dr. Hayes's apologetic smile burned into the darkness. *I'm taking the Dean position at Columbia.* I sat up abruptly, my heart hammering against my ribs like a frantic, trapped bird. I paced the length of my bedroom, dragging my fingernails heavily through my scalp until my roots ached. I opened my laptop, staring at the title page of my manuscript, and a sudden, violent shudder racked my entire body. I slammed the lid shut. I dropped to the floor, pressing my back against the cold radiator. I hugged myself tightly, rocking side to side in the pitch black. My breathing came in ragged, uneven gasps. The walls of my tiny apartment felt like they were inching closer, threatening to physically crush me.

The loud bass of the campus pub vibrated through the sticky table, but Julian heard none of it. His friends were laughing, clinking pint glasses, celebrating the end of the week. Julian stared unblinkingly at the condensation dripping down his glass. Professor Chen’s email from three hours ago was a brand burned into his retinas. *My lab is relocating to Geneva.* Julian’s hand shot out, gripping his glass so tightly his knuckles paled. He brought the rim to his mouth, but his throat seized. He set it down abruptly, knocking over a salt shaker. A cold sweat plastered his shirt to his spine. He excused himself, stumbling toward the restroom. He locked himself in a graffitied stall, leaning his forehead against the cool, painted metal door. His chest heaved. He bit down hard on his own wrist, using the sharp physical sting to anchor himself as the room spun wildly.

The administrative assistant told me to wait on the leather sofa. I sat rigidly, my eyes locked on the tower of flattened cardboard boxes stacked just inside Dr. Patel’s office door. A high-pitched ringing started in my right ear, steadily growing louder. I rubbed my sweaty palms violently against the thighs of my corduroy pants, back and forth, the friction generating a burning heat that I ignored. *He can't leave. He's the only one who understands the algorithms.* I leaned forward, resting my elbows on my knees, and buried my hands in my hair. I pulled downward, hard. The air in the reception area felt impossibly thick, tasting like dust and stale coffee. I bounced my right leg, my boot hammering a relentless rhythm into the floorboards. Every time I heard the distinct sound of packing tape ripping from inside his office, my stomach violently contracted.

Elias stared at the red 'D-' on his physics midterm, the fluorescent lights humming like a swarm of angry wasps in his ears. He dragged his fingernails across his scalp, pulling at the roots of his hair until his eyes watered. If the velocity is constant... The formula mocked him, looping endlessly behind his eyes. He pressed his palms against his temples, trying to physically crush the memory of his confident swagger walking into the exam room. The crumpled paper laid on the desk, its red ink bleeding into the white fibers, felt like a branding iron pressed against his chest. He stood abruptly, knocking his chair back, and paced the length of the empty classroom. Every time he closed his eyes, he saw his father’s expectant smile waiting at the dinner table tonight. A jagged breath tore from his throat.

I haven't slept since Tuesday. The digital clock blinks 3:14 AM, but all I see is the '62/100' circled twice on my history thesis. I toss onto my left side, tangling my legs in the damp sheets, but the ghost of my professor’s scrawled note—"lacks fundamental understanding"—burns behind my eyelids. I punch my pillow, flipping it over, but the cool side offers no relief. My heart hammers an erratic rhythm against my ribs, a trapped bird slamming into glass. I sit up, my fingers digging into the mattress. Why didn't I read the secondary sources? Why did I think my argument was clever? The questions circle like buzzards, picking at the raw edges of my confidence. I grip the edge of the desk, knuckles white, gasping for air in a room that suddenly feels entirely devoid of oxygen.

The chatter of the coffee shop was deafening, but Maya only heard the roar of the ocean in her ears. The screen of her laptop glowed with a single, undeniable 'F'. She had skipped meals for this coding project. She had ignored calls from home. Now, she gnawed viciously on her thumbnail, tasting copper as the skin broke. She didn't stop. The metallic tang mixed with the stale coffee on her tongue. "Hey, Maya, how did you do?" someone asked cheerfully from the next table. Maya flinched, her shoulders jumping up to her ears. She forced her jaw closed, her teeth grinding together so hard a dull ache blossomed in her jawline. She couldn't speak. If she opened her mouth, she knew she would just scream and never, ever stop. She stared at the flashing cursor until her vision blurred completely.

The subway rattled, swaying me against the cold metal pole. Deep inside my backpack, folded into a tiny, sharp square, was the chemistry exam. Just a '45'. The numbers flashed like neon signs every time I blinked. I clamped my hands over my ears, trying to block out the screeching tracks, but the real noise was entirely inside my own skull. Stupid. Worthless. Fraud. The words chanted in a rhythmic loop, syncing perfectly with the clatter of the train wheels. I squeezed my eyes shut, my breath coming in short, shallow hitches that burned my throat. I could feel the exam paper radiating heat through the heavy canvas of my bag, scorching my spine. I shifted away, pressing my face against the chilled glass of the window, desperately wishing the glass would shatter and let the rushing tunnel wind scour my brain clean.

Julian leaned his forehead against the cold metal of locker 402. In his trembling hand was the essay he’d spent three weeks writing, marked with a bold 'C'. His chest heaved in rapid, uneven spasms. He shoved the paper into his backpack, zipped it, then instantly unzipped it to check the grade again. Still a 'C'. He slammed the locker shut, the metallic bang echoing down the empty corridor. He began to walk, but his knees felt completely hollow. He stopped, leaned against the tiled wall, and slid down until he hit the linoleum floor. He curled his arms around his knees, burying his face in the dark space between them. Every time he tried to take a deep breath, an invisible vice tightened around his ribs, squeezing until he choked on a dry, soundless sob. The essay felt like a living parasite, eating away at his insides.

My mother is frying chicken, humming a tune that feels like sandpaper scraping across my brain. I stare at the 'B-' on my art portfolio—the portfolio I needed for the scholarship. The red ink glares at me. I trace the outline of the letter with my fingernail, pressing so hard the paper tears. My stomach churns, a violent sea of acid and dread. "Set the table, sweetie," Mom calls out. I stand up, but the room tilts. I grab the edge of the counter, my knuckles turning translucent. You blew it. The thought is a physical blow to my abdomen. I double over slightly, clutching my stomach. I can feel the 'B-' etched into my skin, marking me as a failure. I walk to the sink, turn on the cold water, and splash my face, but the icy shock does absolutely nothing to quiet the screaming in my head.

Sarah sat perfectly still in the back corner of the library, the glow of her tablet illuminating her pale face. 'Score: 510'. The law school admission test results were in. She didn't cry. Instead, she began plucking a single strand of hair from her left temple, wrapping it around her index finger, and pulling until it snapped. Then she found another. And another. A small pile of brown hairs gathered on the oak table. Her jaw was locked tight, muscles bulging at the corners. She imagined her future—the corner office, the courtroom—dissolving into ash and slipping through her fingers. She pressed the heels of her hands hard into her eye sockets until bursts of colored light exploded in the darkness. Her chest felt utterly hollowed out, scraped clean by a jagged spoon, leaving nothing but an echoing, cavernous ache that threatened to swallow her whole.

The rain is soaking through my jacket, but I barely feel the chill. All I feel is the burning weight of the transcript folded in my pocket. 'Academic Probation'. The words echo with every sloshing step I take on the pavement. I kick violently at a puddle, sending muddy water splashing up my jeans. Why didn't I study that weekend? Why did I go out? I punch my own thigh, hard, welcoming the dull, throbbing pain that follows. It’s a distraction from the relentless, gnawing beast in my chest. I tilt my head back, letting the rain hit my face, hoping it might wash away the suffocating shame. But the beast just tightens its claws around my lungs, making every breath a battle. I wrap my arms tightly around myself, shivering uncontrollably, trapped entirely inside a nightmare I built with my own two hands.

Leo stared at the canvas, the red 'Incomplete/F' sticky note fluttering in the drafty studio. He picked up his palette knife, his fingers slick with sweat.
