I scratch at the old burn scar on my left forearm, my fingernails digging deeply into the puckered tissue until a thin line of blood beads up. "Look at this vintage dress!" she calls out. I swallow a lump of ash that isn't there, unable to pry my eyes away from the blackened beam, trapped forever in that smoke-filled night.

Julian paced the length of the study, his footsteps echoing in the cavernous room. His brother, Arthur, sat calmly in the leather armchair, pouring a glass of scotch. "It’s a simple condition, Jules. We live here together for one year, and the deed is ours." Arthur smiled, but it didn't reach his eyes. Julian’s breath hitched. He grabbed the back of a dining chair, his knuckles white, his chest rising and falling in rapid, shallow bursts. One year. 365 days trapped in this isolated manor with the man who had ruined his marriage and stolen his career. Julian’s vision swam, black spots dancing at the edges of his sight. He bit the inside of his cheek until he tasted copper, forcing back the bile rising in his throat. He looked at the heavy oak doors, the deadbolts, and felt invisible walls closing in around his throat.

"We should appraise the emerald necklace first," Jane suggests, flipping through the directory. I stare down at the worn carpet, my heart pounding a frantic, deafening rhythm against my eardrums. My palms are slick with sweat, and I rub them aggressively against my jeans. I know exactly where the necklace is. It’s sitting in a pawn shop window three towns over, sold to cover a gambling debt I swore I had paid off. I wrap my arms around my stomach, bending slightly forward as a wave of intense nausea rolls over me. When Jane checks the velvet box in the safe, she’ll find it empty. She’ll look at me with that same profound disgust Gran always had. I pace toward the window, dragging my nails down the side of my face, silently begging the sky to send a lightning bolt to burn the entire house down to ashes.

The lawyer’s voice buzzed like television static. Felix sat perfectly still on the velvet couch, staring at the dust motes dancing in the shaft of afternoon light. His sister squeezed his hand in celebration, her joy radiating through the dusty living room. They had finally inherited the estate. But all Felix could feel was a heavy, suffocating anvil resting squarely on his chest. His grandmother was the only person who had ever understood him, the only one who had anchored him to the world. Now, she was just an urn on the mantle. He squeezed his eyes shut, but tears leaked out anyway, hot and relentless. He pulled his knees to his chest, wrapping his arms around them in a tight ball, rocking slightly. The massive, empty house stretched out around him, an endless cavern of silence promising to swallow him whole now that his protector was gone.

Elias dug his fingernails into his palms until crescent moons of red blossomed against his skin. The humming of the fluorescent lights in Dr. Aris's clinic felt like a drill boring directly into his skull. He couldn't sit still, shifting his weight, trying to escape the electric spasms shooting up his spine. The woman across from him dropped a familiar orange pillbox. As she scrambled to pick it up, Elias recognized the distinct hexagonal tablets of Myroxim. Their eyes locked, and Elias saw his own sleepless nights mirrored in her sunken, shadowed gaze. "You get the midnight tremors too?" she whispered, her voice fragile. Elias nodded, his throat tight, remembering the hours spent thrashing against tangled bedsheets, begging the darkness for a single moment of silence. For the first time, the heavy, suffocating iron band around his chest loosened slightly, though the tremors remained.

I kept my hands shoved deep into my coat pockets, desperate to hide the violent shaking that no sweater could warm. The coffee shop was loud, a chaotic blur of noise that amplified the relentless ringing in my ears. I ordered a black tea, my voice cracking, and accidentally bumped into the man beside me. His sleeve hiked up, revealing the web-like pattern of violet veins stretching up his forearm—the exact same unnatural roadmap etched into my own skin. "It doesn't fade," he murmured, quickly pulling his sleeve down, his jaw clenching so hard I thought his teeth might crack. "Neither does the ringing," I replied, pressing the heels of my hands against my temples, trying to crush the noise inside my head. We stood there in the bustling line, two ghosts haunted by the same invisible fire, locked in a private, silent scream.

Maya paced the hallway outside the community center, her breathing shallow and ragged. Every step sent a jolt of ice water through her joints, a cruel reminder of her failing body. She hated the pitying looks of healthy people, the way their eyes slid away from her cane. She slammed her back against the brick wall, sliding down to the floor, pulling her knees to her chest to stop the sudden, violent shivering. A young man with a matching silver cane sat on the bench opposite her, his knuckles white as he gripped the handle. "Feltters Syndrome?" he asked, his voice rough, eyes darting to her hands. Maya squeezed her eyes shut as another wave of phantom fire tore through her nerves. She nodded, digging her teeth into her lower lip to keep from crying out. "I thought I was the only one," he breathed.

I stared at the diner menu until the letters swam together, my stomach twisting into familiar, sharp knots. I hadn’t eaten a full meal in three months, terrified of the violent spasms that always followed. When the bell above the door chimed, a woman walked in, pressing a hand flat against her abdomen, her face a mask of exhaustion and tight lines. She slid into the booth across from me. "User BlueEcho?" she asked. I nodded, wiping a bead of cold sweat from my hairline. "It feels like swallowing ground glass," I blurted out, unable to hold back the dark thoughts that kept me awake until dawn. "And breathing feels like inhaling embers," she finished, her fingers tracing the edge of her water glass. I dropped my head into my hands, the sheer weight of our shared nightmare pressing down on my shoulders.

The pharmacy line stretched endlessly, and David felt every second as a physical blow to his temples. He leaned heavily against the shelving unit, closing his eyes to block out the harsh light that made his vision swim. His bones ached with a deep, hollow cold that no blanket could cure. The woman in front of him argued with the pharmacist, her voice bordering on a sob. "Please, the insurance must cover the Kaelen-Drop. I can't go back to the waking blackouts." David’s head snapped up. He stepped forward, his heart hammering against his ribs like a trapped bird. "You have the blackouts?" he interrupted, his voice trembling. She spun around, her eyes wide, ringed with the same bruised purple as his own. "Every time I close my eyes," she whispered. David gripped the counter, the room spinning around their shared, waking nightmare.

I sat on the park bench, my hands covering my ears, trying to block out the overwhelming roar of the wind. To anyone else, it was a gentle breeze; to my frayed nervous system, it was a siren. I rocked back and forth, biting the inside of my cheek until it tasted like copper. A man sat down on the opposite end of the bench, moving with deliberate, robotic stiffness. He was wearing noise-canceling headphones and thick, dark glasses despite the overcast sky. A sudden crack of thunder sounded in the distance. We both flinched violently, folding in on ourselves, gasping for air as sensory overload struck like a physical blow. He pulled off his headphones, his chest heaving, tears streaming down his face. "Corvis Disease?" he asked, his voice barely a whisper. I could only nod, trapped in the cage of my own senses.

The elevator jerked to a sudden halt between the fourteenth and fifteenth floors. Marcus immediately dropped his briefcase, his breath hitching as the metallic smell of the small space triggered a wave of intense nausea. He pressed his face against the cool steel wall, trying to ground himself, but the phantom falling sensation—the hallmark of his rare vestibular disorder—sent the room spinning wildly. Beside him, a woman gasped, sinking to her knees and clutching her head as if it might split open. "The floor is dropping," she whimpered, her eyes wide and unseeing. "It's not real, it's the Vernal Vertigo," Marcus choked out, crawling toward her. He grabbed her hand, anchoring her to the ground. "Hold on to me." They sat in the dim light, two strangers clinging to each other as their brains lied to them, trapped in a relentless, spinning void.

The heart monitor beeped in a slow, rhythmic taunt. I lay in the hospital bed, staring at the ceiling tiles, counting the dots to stop my mind from racing. Every breath felt like inhaling shards of ice, a symptom the doctors still couldn't explain. I dragged myself out of bed, dragging my IV pole into the empty hallway, desperate to escape the sterile room. I found another patient by the window, a girl no older than twenty, wrapping her arms tightly around her chest, rocking slowly. "Does the ice ever melt?" she asked softly, without turning around. My breath caught in my throat. I stepped beside her, looking out at the city lights. "Not yet," I whispered, gripping the cold metal of my IV pole until my knuckles ached, overwhelmed by the crushing reality that neither of us could wake up from this dream.

As the plane ascended, the cabin pressure shifted, and Arthur squeezed his eyes shut. A high-pitched whine began in his left ear, quickly escalating into a blinding pressure behind his eyes. He dug his fingers into the armrests, his breathing fast and shallow. He just had to make it through the flight. The man in the seat next to him suddenly groaned, pressing both palms fiercely against his eyes. "The pressure," the stranger gasped, pulling a specialized pressurized inhaler from his bag. Arthur’s eyes widened. He reached into his own coat pocket and pulled out an identical silver device. They locked eyes over the tray table, a silent understanding passing between them. Arthur took a shaky breath, the raw, gnawing fear in his gut easing just a fraction. He wasn't the only one carrying this invisible, heavy stone through the sky.

I kept my head down on the subway, hiding the involuntary muscle ticks that ripped through my jaw. Every jolt of the train sent a shockwave of electricity down my spine. I gripped the pole so hard my forearm cramped, praying nobody was staring at my erratic movements. A woman stepped onto the train at the next stop, stumbling as a tremor seized her leg. She caught herself on the seat across from me, her face flushed with embarrassment and pure exhaustion. As she adjusted her grip, I saw the distinctive copper brace on her wrist, a custom orthotic for Lenox-Ward Syndrome. I tapped my own identical brace against the metal pole. She looked up, her panicked breathing slowing as her eyes met mine. For a fleeting moment, the train car felt less like a prison, even as another violent spark danced down my spine.

Elena shredded the edge of her appointment card, leaving a pile of paper snow on the floor. Her mind was a chaotic storm of worst-case scenarios, playing out her inevitable decline in vivid, horrifying detail. She couldn't sleep; she couldn't eat. The heavy wooden door opened, and a man walked out of the counselor's office. He looked hollowed out, his shoulders slumped as if carrying a physical weight. He stopped near her chair, pulling up his collar, revealing a patch of silver, scaly skin on his neck. Elena gasped, reaching up to touch the silk scarf hiding her own identical patch. "They told you it's progressive, didn't they?" she whispered, her voice cracking. He nodded slowly, his eyes brimming with unshed tears. Elena buried her face in her hands, the suffocating reality of their shared, shrinking future pressing down on her chest.

I sat at the library desk surrounded by towering stacks of medical journals, tracing the lines of text until the words blurred into meaningless shapes. My head throbbed, a relentless drumbeat warning of an impending migraine. I swept a stack of books off the table in a burst of sheer frustration, burying my face in my arms. A hand tapped my shoulder. I looked up to see a woman holding a heavily bookmarked copy of Rare Autoimmune Pathologies. "You're researching the Omenn variant, aren't you?" she asked softly. I nodded, wiping at the tears of pure exhaustion leaking from the corners of my eyes. She pulled out the chair next to me and sat down, her own hands trembling slightly as she opened the book. "I’ve been looking for three years," she said. I leaned closer, my racing heartbeat finding a steady, shared rhythm in the silence.

Elias stared at the lock screen on the stranger’s phone resting on the café table. It was the same dimpled smile, the same crooked baseball cap Elias had kissed yesterday. His jaw clenched so hard his teeth ground audibly. He dug his fingernails into his own thighs under the table, leaving deep crescent indentations through his jeans. "So," the stranger, Marcus, said cheerfully. "He told me he was at a work retreat this weekend." Elias felt a violent churning in his gut, like he had swallowed broken glass. He couldn't blink, couldn't look away from that photo. The café noise faded into a dull roar, echoing the relentless thumping behind his temples. He opened his mouth to speak, but only a dry, ragged gasp came out. He squeezed his eyes shut, but the image of that shared smile burned vividly behind his eyelids, refusing to give him a moment of peace.

The woman beside me at the gallery smelled of sandalwood—Leo’s scent. I complimented her scarf. She laughed, touching the silk. "My boyfriend got it for me in Paris last month." I stopped breathing. Paris. Our anniversary trip. I stared at the abstract painting until the colors bled into a spinning blur. A cold sweat broke out across my neck. I pressed my knuckles against my mouth, stifling a noise that felt like it was tearing my throat apart. "He has great taste," I whispered, my voice vibrating with a high, unnatural tremor. I backed away, my chest rising and falling in shallow, frantic hitches. Every memory from that trip replayed in my mind as a grotesque distortion. I wanted to claw my own skin off, just to escape the phantom feeling of his hands still lingering on my waist.

Sarah watched the golden retriever chase a tennis ball, her fingers gripping the cold chain-link fence until her knuckles turned stark white. The man standing nearby called the dog 'Barnaby.' It was her dog. Well, Greg’s dog, the one she had bought him for Christmas. "He’s a rescue," the man chuckled. "My fiancé, Greg, surprised me with him." Sarah’s stomach dropped into an endless, dizzying void. She dug the heel of her boot into the mud, trying to ground herself. Her pulse hammered against her eardrums, loud and erratic. She wanted to scream, to run until her lungs gave out. Instead, she stood frozen, swallowing rising bile. She imagined Greg’s lips pressing against this man’s forehead. The thought was a physical weight, crushing her ribs inward, making every drawn breath a colossal, exhausting effort she barely had the strength to manage.

I recognized the distinctive blue ribbons tied to the suitcase handle. I reached for it just as another hand grabbed the opposite side. We both looked up. "Oh, sorry," she smiled. "Waiting for my husband. He uses these tacky ribbons." She pointed to a man walking toward us from the food court. Julian. My Julian. The ground beneath the baggage carousel seemed to tilt. My knees buckled, forcing me to lean heavily against the metal barrier. I couldn't tear my eyes away from him. My jaw locked tight. A high-pitched ringing drowned out the terminal announcements. I pressed both hands over my ears, screwing my eyes shut, but it didn't stop the relentless, heavy pounding in my skull. I desperately wanted to sink through the floor, to be swallowed entirely by the concrete, rather than exist in this sickening collision of realities.

The notification lit up the bench between them. David stared at the screen of the other man’s phone. A text from Babe, accompanied by a photo David himself had taken of Mark at the beach last weekend. David’s towel slipped from his shoulders. He felt a sudden, violent chill, his teeth chattering uncontrollably despite the heavy steam of the locker room. The other man, drying his hair, smiled down at the screen. "Love this guy," he muttered to himself. David’s hands balled into tight fists, his nails cutting half-moons into his palms. He retreated into a bathroom stall, locking the door and sliding down the tiled wall. He pulled his knees to his chest, rocking back and forth. He clamped a hand over his mouth to muffle the harsh, ragged sobs that were tearing violently up from his chest, shaking his entire frame.

The woman sitting across from me on the commuter train was knitting a sweater. It was the exact shade of maroon yarn I had helped Alex pick out at the craft store last month. "Making it for my girlfriend," she noticed me looking. "Alex is always cold." The train lurched. I grabbed the edge of my seat, my knuckles popping. The air in the carriage suddenly felt thicker than water. I tugged at the collar of my shirt, gasping quietly. I could see them together, sharing the apartment I paid half the rent for. I bit down on my lower lip so hard I tasted a sharp, metallic copper tang. My leg bounced at a frantic, uncontrollable pace. I stared at the blurring trees outside the window, my reflection ghost-like in the glass. Every mile the train moved forward felt like another heavy stone placed directly on my chest.

Nina stood paralyzed in the cereal aisle, staring at the woman comparing prices on oatmeal. The woman had just taken a call on speakerphone, and the voice echoing from the tinny speaker belonged to Liam. Her Liam. Telling this woman he couldn't wait to see her tonight. Nina’s grocery basket slipped from her fingers, clattering loudly against the linoleum. She stumbled backward into a display of canned beans. Her vision tunneled, the bright fluorescent lights overhead pulsing in time with her racing, erratic heartbeat. She wrapped her arms around her own torso, squeezing tightly as if trying to hold her splintering ribs together. She squeezed her eyes shut, shaking her head side to side in a rapid, jerky motion. "No, no, no," she whispered under her breath, a relentless loop that did nothing to stop the room from spinning wildly out of control.

We both reached for the dropped concert ticket at the same time. He laughed, flashing a familiar silver ring on his thumb. I froze. I had custom-ordered that ring for Sam. "Nice ring," I croaked out, my throat tight and dry as sandpaper. "Thanks, my boyfriend got it for me," he smiled, pointing toward the bar. Sam was standing there, ordering drinks. The heavy bass from the speakers vibrated through my boots, but it was nothing compared to the violent shuddering in my own limbs. I backed away into the crowd. Faces smeared into unrecognizable shapes. I scratched frantically at my forearms, leaving angry red welts on the skin. I couldn't breathe. I shoved my way toward the exit, tripping over feet, desperate to escape the suffocating heat of the venue and the image of Sam turning to hand that stranger my drink.

Dr. Evans’s waiting room was quiet until the receptionist called out, "Emergency contact for Maya Lin?" Two people stood up simultaneously. Chloe locked eyes with the man across the room. "I'm her husband," he said, stepping forward. Chloe’s legs gave out. She collapsed back into the plastic chair, her ears ringing with a shrill, deafening pitch. Maya had told her she was single. They had been looking at apartments yesterday. Chloe grabbed handfuls of her own hair, pulling until the roots burned. She stared at the floor tiles, counting the scuff marks, over and over, trying to force her brain to process anything other than the words her husband. Her chest heaved. She bit into the side of her thumb, applying pressure until she felt the bone, trying to replace the overwhelming, invisible weight crushing her spirit with a physical sensation she could actually control.

The new member of our book club set her copy of the novel on the table. Inside the front cover was a handwritten dedication. To my shining star, love forever, Chris. I recognized the looping 'C'. It was the exact same signature on the birthday card currently sitting on my nightstand. The tea I was drinking turned to ash in my mouth. I swallowed heavily, a severe lump forming in my throat that refused to budge. I gripped the armrests of my chair, my body rigid, vibrating with an intense, restless energy. I couldn't look at her face. I stared fixedly at the book, my breathing growing shallow and rapid. I needed to stand up. I needed to break a window. I excused myself, locking the bathroom door behind me, where I leaned over the sink and dry-heaved until my ribs ached.

The ride-share stopped to pick up a second passenger. As the young woman slid into the backseat, her phone rang with a custom ringtone—a highly specific, obscure jazz song. Javier snapped his head toward her. Only his boyfriend, Tomas, used that obscure track. "Hey babe," the woman answered, her voice dripping with affection. "I'm in the car." Javier’s stomach twisted violently. He pressed his forehead against the cold, vibrating window of the car. He closed his eyes, but the darkness offered no relief. His foot tapped a frantic, irregular rhythm against the floor mats. He wrapped his arms around his waist, bending forward slightly as if he had taken a physical blow to the abdomen. Every time she laughed at something Tomas said on the line, Javier flinched, curling tighter into himself, wishing he could dissolve completely into the upholstery.

We were sitting next to each other on the flight. The guy in the window seat opened his gallery, and a photo popped up. It was him, kissing Elena in front of the Eiffel Tower. The timestamp was from this morning. Elena was supposed to be at her sister's house. I sat completely paralyzed, staring blankly at the tray table. A sudden rush of heat enveloped my entire body, followed immediately by freezing chills. I dug my fingers into the synthetic fabric of my seat cushion until my nails threatened to break. The roar of the jet engines faded into a distant hum, replaced by the rushing blood roaring in my ears. I squeezed my eyes shut, replaying every text, every phone call, every touch, tearing them apart in my mind. I wanted to pry the cabin door open at thirty thousand feet just to let the freezing air rush in.
